question: The German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) maintains a bureaucracy cost index. In July, the index jumped by 2.4 per cent on the previous month – its sharpest increase ever. According to reports, Destatis attributes this significant increase to the introduction of sustainability reporting under the EU’s CSRD1. According to expert calculations, an increase of 2.

4 per cent would give rise to an additional burden of over EUR 1.5 billion per year. It thus follows that a significant proportion of Germany’s total compliance costs are attributable to the CSRD. Germany claims that it has chosen to implement the CSRD on a like-for-like basis. Accordingly, the quantified compliance costs would appear to have been caused solely by the transposition of EU law.

The transposition of the directive means a considerable increase in red tape, not only for Germany but also for the EU as a whole, which runs counter to the Commission's goal of increasing competitiveness. 1.
What calculations has the Commission made as to the compliance costs caused by the CSRD?
Does the Commission agree with the conclusion, based on the information provided by Germany, that the initially estimated compliance costs are wholly attributable to the transposition of EU law?

Are the additional costs incurred as a result of the CSRD being included in the current review of the overall burden, and is the Commission already considering streamlining and assistance measures that go beyond those set out in the answers to the frequently asked questions of 7 August 2024?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.4.2025) The first set of calculations made by the Commission on the costs of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD)1 were explained under the impact assessment document accompanying the CSRD proposal2.

In this document, the total incremental recurring costs of reporting against sustainability reporting standards in all 27 Member States were estimated at EUR 2.1 billion per year, plus additional recurrent costs for audit and assurance and the one-off implementation costs. Subsequently, when adopting the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) Delegated Act, the Commission estimated EUR 1.

7 billion in annual recurring costs across the EU for reporting against ESRS3. This recurring costs estimate shows a reduction compared to the estimate in the 2021 CSRD impact assessment as a result of various simplifications made. On 26 February the Commission adopted legislative proposals to modify the CSRD, as part of the ‘Omnibus’ initiative to reduce administrative burden on companies.

The Commission estimates that the proposed modifications would exempt about 80% of companies from reporting under the CSRD and lead to CSRD/ESRS reporting cost savings of EUR 1.2 billion per year, plus savings on the related audit and assurance costs. Beyond this, companies would also benefit from being exempted from taxonomy reporting and future simplifications of the ESRS.

As set out in more detail in the assessment accompanying the omnibus proposal,4 the combined cost savings resulting from the proposed changes to the CSRD scope (including the exemptions this would bring for Taxonomy reporting), plus the modifications of the future ESRS, have been estimated to amount to EUR 4.4 billion per year.
